sounds.name: Endless Oscillator
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s drone music
sounds.blurb: VCO B’s oscillator, patched into EXT.AUDIO, sounds without its envelope: a held tone that never stops, gliding to each new key while VCO A plucks over it.
sounds.how: VCO B’s osc out is the oscillator itself, before its envelope and VCA. Patched into EXT. AUDIO in, it reaches the mixer on a channel of its own that no key opens or closes: it sounds all the time, at the pitch of the last key. Portamento makes it glide from one to the next, under VCO A playing as usual.

steps.title: A pluck
steps.why:
VCO A on triangle. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 4.
- Listen for: short, soft notes.

steps.title: An endless tone
steps.why:
VCO B on saw, VOL 0, with −1 SUB on. Patch VCO B’s osc out to EXT. AUDIO in. EXT.AUDIO VOL 6.
- Listen for: a buzzing tone that holds between the plucks and changes pitch with each.

steps.title: Glide
steps.why:
PORTAMENTO 5. Both FREQ to 4.5, RES 4.
- Listen for: the held tone sliding slowly to each new note, darker now.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the plucks and the glide in a wide space.

context.mix.ext.vol: In this sound: how loud the endless tone is.

tweaks.hear: The held tone a fourth below the plucks.
Slow, sirening slides.

sounds.name: Modulator Sync
sounds.ref: In the style of noise music
sounds.blurb: VCO A hard-synced to a Papa Srapa’s modulator: a fixed, buzzing pulse whose tone the keys colour.
sounds.how: Sync restarts an oscillator each time a signal rises. The usual master is the other VCO, but any square will do: a Papa Srapa’s modulator out is one, from slow to buzzing. Synced to it, VCO A sounds at the modulator’s rate, a low buzz, while VCO A’s own pitch, from the keys, decides the tone inside each cycle: the keys play colour, not notes.

steps.title: A bright saw
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, SUSTAIN 9.
- Listen for: a saw following the keys.

steps.title: A buzzing master
steps.why:
Drone 3: 1 / 10 on, rate 9. The voice stays closed; only its modulator is used.
- Listen for: nothing new yet: the modulator runs silently.

steps.title: Sync
steps.why:
Patch Drone 3’s modulator out to VCO A’s sync.
- Listen for: a fixed, low buzz; each key now changes its colour, not its pitch.

steps.title: Sweep the colour
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to VCO A’s cv, CV AMT 3, LFO A rate 6.
- Listen for: the buzz’s colour sweeping slowly up and down, a vowel-like sync sweep.

context.d3.rate: In this sound: the pitch you hear, set by the modulator.

tweaks.hear: The buzz slowing into a stuttering motor.
A slow, rhythmic restart: a clicking, retriggered saw.

sounds.name: Srapa Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Berlin-school sequencer music
sounds.blurb: The sequencer plays a Papa Srapa voice as a bassline, its FM trilling every note: a sequence no VCO is used for.
sounds.how: The sequencer’s cv out and gate out can play anything with a pitch input and a gate. A Papa Srapa has both, so the pulser can step it through a five-note line on its own. Its FM, set shallow and fast, gives each note a burbling trill. The pulser runs on its own: this sound plays without a key held.

steps.title: A low square
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 6: PITCH 6.92, so its tone sits on C3. ATT 0, RLS 3, VOL 7, PAN 0.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the voice is closed.

steps.title: Sequence it
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s cv out to Drone 6’s cv and its gate out to Drone 6’s GATE. Steps 0, 1.17, 2, 1.67, 0.5. Pulser 6.
- Listen for: a five-note bass pattern played on its own.

steps.title: Burble
steps.why:
Drone 6: FM on, MOD 1, DIVIDER 5, 1 / 10 on, rate 6.
- Listen for: each note trilling and burbling.

steps.title: Echo
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 4. TIME on both sides, program 1. X 4, Y 4, Z 3, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: the pattern echoing in the dark.

context.d6.mod: In this sound: how wide each note’s trill is.

tweaks.hear: Each note chopped into a stutter.
A rest in the pattern, which turns the groove.

sounds.name: Wandering Chords
sounds.ref: In the style of generative ambient music
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa’s sample and hold throws a drone’s eye to a new brightness every few seconds, so its upper chord jumps to a new, unpredictable place over a still bass.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s S&H, with nothing in its clock, is clocked by its own modulator, so it hands out a new random voltage at the modulator’s rate even while the voice is silent. Into a classic drone’s CV it moves the light on the eye up and down from where the LIGHT knob leaves it, and the generators whose MOD is on jump with it: a chord that keeps wandering.

steps.title: A drone chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: generator 1 to F1, 2 to C3, 3 to A3, 4 to E4, 5 to C6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 5, RLS 7, PAN 0.
- Listen for: an F major seventh, spread wide.

steps.title: Half-light the eye
steps.why:
MOD on generators 3, 4 and 5. Drone 4’s LIGHT 5, CV 10.
- Listen for: the upper three rising six semitones: room for the light to move both ways.

steps.title: Random light
steps.why:
Patch Drone 3’s S&H out to Drone 4’s CV. Drone 3’s rate 2.
- Listen for: the upper chord jumping to a new place every few seconds.

steps.title: Blur it
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 7, BLEND 5. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: each jump melting into the last.

context.d3.rate: In this sound: how often the chord wanders.
context.d4.cv: In this sound: how far each jump can go.

tweaks.hear: Small, microtonal drifts instead of jumps.

sounds.name: Glitch Echo
sounds.ref: In the style of glitch electronica
sounds.blurb: A sample and hold jumps TIME’s delay length at random, so the echoes of a plain melody leap in pitch and stutter like a skipping CD.
sounds.how: Jumping a delay’s time while it holds sound makes its repeats skip and bend. The effector’s cv y moves Y, which on TIME is the delay time; a Papa Srapa’s sample and hold gives it a new random length at its modulator’s rate. The dry melody stays clean while its echoes glitch.

steps.title: A plain melody
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 4. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 4. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: a simple, hollow tune.

steps.title: An echo
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 6, Y 3, Z 3, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: a steady, repeating echo.

steps.title: Glitch it
steps.why:
Patch Drone 6’s S&H out to the effector’s cv y. Drone 6’s 1 / 10 off, rate 6.
- Listen for: the echoes jumping in pitch and stuttering once or twice a second.

context.d6.rate: In this sound: how often the delay jumps.

tweaks.hear: Jumps many times a second: a granular smear.

sounds.name: Pulse-Width FM
sounds.ref: In the style of IDM keys
sounds.blurb: VCO B, unheard, moves VCO A’s pulse width at audio rate: a reedy, ring-modulated tone that changes character as VCO B is retuned.
sounds.how: Pulse-width modulation is usually slow. At audio rate it becomes a kind of FM: the width changes hundreds of times a cycle, adding sidebands. VCO B’s osc out into VCO A’s pwm input does that; both follow the keys, so the sound stays in tune, and VCO B’s TUNE picks the colour.

steps.title: A square
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 5. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 4.
- Listen for: a plain, hollow square.

steps.title: Move its width at audio rate
steps.why:
VCO B on sine, VOL 0. Patch VCO B’s osc out to VCO A’s pwm, PWM 8.
- Listen for: the square turning reedy and nasal.

steps.title: Pick the colour
steps.why:
VCO B’s OCT LOW, so it moves the width three octaves below.
- Listen for: a growling, buzzing reed.

steps.title: Room
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 6. CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3. X 2, Y 3, Z 4, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: the reed in a small room.

context.vb.tune: In this sound: the colour of the reed.

tweaks.hear: Beating, shifting partials: the reed going in and out of tune with itself.

tweaks.try: Set VCO B back to OCT +3
tweaks.hear: A brighter, glassier ring.

sounds.name: Metal Scrape
sounds.ref: In the style of industrial metal scrapes
sounds.blurb: VCO B’s oscillator swings a Papa Srapa’s pitch across ten octaves at audio rate: a scraping, clanging metal sound that the keys retune.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s cv input moves its pitch an octave a volt, and VCO B’s osc out swings ±5 V: patched together, VCO B throws the square up and down five octaves each way, hundreds of times a second. That is frequency modulation far past polite, and it scrapes and clangs. The keys change VCO B’s pitch, and so the metal.

steps.title: A square tone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 3: PITCH 5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 1, RLS 5, VOL 5, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a plain low square on each key.

steps.title: Scrape it
steps.why:
VCO B on triangle, OCT LOW, VOL 0. Patch VCO B’s osc out to Drone 3’s cv.
- Listen for: the square shattered into a scraping, metallic clang.

steps.title: Tame the top
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 5. CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1, Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: a darker, ringing metal in a big space.

context.vb.oct: In this sound: LOW, so VCO B swings the pitch slowly enough to hear it scrape.

tweaks.hear: A dense, hissing noise.

sounds.name: Envelope on the Eye
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s drone music
sounds.blurb: VCO A’s envelope, looping while a key is held, flickers the light on a drone’s eye, so its upper generators pulse up and down: a drone that throbs while you hold it.
sounds.how: A 42N VCO envelope with LOOP on cycles for as long as its key is held, and its env out can go anywhere. Here VCO A is silent; its looping envelope goes into a classic drone’s CV jack, lighting the eye in pulses. Only the generators whose MOD is on rise with it, so the drone’s top swoops while its bottom holds.

steps.title: A drone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 5: generator 1 to G1, 2 to D3, 3 to G3, 4 to B4, 5 to D6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 3, RLS 6, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a G major chord.

steps.title: A looping envelope
steps.why:
Envelope A: LOOP on, ATTACK 6, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 0.
- Listen for: nothing yet: VCO A is silent.

steps.title: Onto the eye
steps.why:
Patch Envelope A’s env out to Drone 5’s CV. MOD on generators 4 and 5. Drone 5’s CV 4.
- Listen for: the top two generators swooping up and back, over and over.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 6, BLEND 4. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: the swoops trailing into the reverb.

context.ea.d: In this sound: with ATTACK, the speed of the swoop.

tweaks.hear: A sharp jump and slow fall: a sighing chord.
Swoops of most of an octave.

sounds.name: Pumping Pad
sounds.ref: In the style of French-house pumping pads
sounds.blurb: A Papa Srapa thump on the right feeds the envelope follower, which opens the left side’s filter on a drone pad: a pad that pulses in time with the beat.
sounds.how: WET OUT R is a signal like any other, so it can feed the PREAMP and the envelope follower. Put a rhythm on the right and a pad on the left, and the follower’s voltage into CV L opens the left filter on every beat. MOD R at 0 keeps the right side out of it, though CV L still reaches it through the normal.

steps.title: A pad on the left
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generator 1 to A1, 2 to E2, 3 to C4, 4 to G4, 5 to B5, PAN −5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 3, RLS 6.
- Listen for: an A minor pad on the left.

steps.title: A thump on the right
steps.why:
Drone 3: PITCH 3.5, AM on, rate 6, PAN +5, VOL 7, ATT 0, RLS 3. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: a low, pulsing thump on the right.

steps.title: Close the left
steps.why:
Left FREQ 3, RES 4. MOD L 6, MOD R 0.
- Listen for: the pad muffled on the left.

steps.title: Let the thump open it
steps.why:
Patch WET OUT R to the PREAMP’s ext. source, PREAMP gain 6, and the envelope follower’s env out to CV L.
- Listen for: the pad swelling open on every thump.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on the left side only, program 1. Z 5, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the pumping pad in a room; the thump dry.

sounds.name: Wobble That Follows
sounds.ref: In the style of dubstep wobble bass
sounds.blurb: VCO B, dropped to OCT LOW and unheard, wobbles the filter at a rate set by the key you play: high notes wobble fast, low notes slow.
sounds.how: An LFO has its own rate, but a VCO follows the keys. VCO B at OCT LOW runs three octaves under the key, which for bass notes is slow enough to hear as a wobble, not a pitch. Patched into CV L, it moves the filter on VCO A’s bass at a rate that rises an octave for every octave you play: an LFO that tracks the keyboard.

steps.title: A bass
steps.why:
VCO A on saw, −1 SUB on. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, SUSTAIN 10, RELEASE 2.
- Listen for: a plain, buzzing bass.

steps.title: A slow VCO
steps.why:
VCO B on triangle, OCT LOW, VOL 0.
- Listen for: nothing new: VCO B is silent, running far below the keys.

steps.title: On the filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 4, RES 6, MOD L and MOD R 4. Patch VCO B’s osc out to CV L.
- Listen for: the bass wobbling, faster on the higher notes.

steps.title: Grit
steps.why:
DIST 4, GAIN 6. MASTER VOLUME 6.
- Listen for: a growling, tracking wobble.

context.vb.tune: In this sound: fine-tunes the wobble’s rate against the note.

tweaks.hear: A hard, on-off wobble.
Audio-rate filter FM: a clangorous growl.

sounds.name: Buzzing Eye
sounds.ref: In the style of drone metal
sounds.blurb: LFO B at ×10, fast enough to be a low tone, flickers a drone’s eye, so its generators pick up a buzzing, growling FM.
sounds.how: LFO B’s ×10 switch takes it up to two hundred cycles a second, into audio. Into a classic drone’s CV, it flickers the light on the eye that fast, and the generators whose MOD is on are frequency-modulated: a buzz and a growl that change with LFO B’s rate.

steps.title: A drone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 2: generator 1 muted, then G2, D4, G4, D6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 3, RLS 6, PAN 0.
- Listen for: an open G fifth chord.

steps.title: Flicker the eye
steps.why:
MOD on all four. LFO B out to Drone 2’s CV, Drone 2’s CV 2. LFO B speed ×10, rate 7, wave 0.
- Listen for: the chord buzzing and growling.

steps.title: Shape it
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 4. VIBE on both sides, program 3 (Resonance flanger). X 5, Y 2, Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: a metallic, sweeping growl.

sounds.name: Thunderstorm
sounds.ref: In the style of radio-drama thunder
sounds.blurb: A low classic drone, VOLT past halfway so its generators cross-modulate into a rumble, rolling through a slowly moving filter, with Papa Srapa rain on top.
sounds.how: Past the middle of VOLT, a classic drone’s generators frequency-modulate one another and the chord turns into noise. Tuned low and filtered dark, that is a roll of thunder; a slow LFO on the filter makes it rumble nearer and further. Drone 3’s noise, panned the other way, is the rain.

steps.title: A low drone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: generators 1, 2 and 3 to C1, F♯2 and C4, 4 and 5 muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 6, RLS 8, VOL 8, PAN −2.
- Listen for: a low, dissonant chord.

steps.title: Thunder
steps.why:
Drone 4’s VOLT 8.
- Listen for: the chord breaking down into a rough, rolling rumble.

steps.title: Roll it
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 3.5. Patch LFO A out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R 3, LFO A rate 5.
- Listen for: the rumble rolling nearer and further.

steps.title: Rain
steps.why:
Drone 3: NOISE 10, ATT 6, RLS 8, VOL 5, PAN +4. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3, X 2, Y 6, Z 7, BLEND 4. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: hissing rain on the right, the storm in a huge space.

sounds.name: Joystick Siren
sounds.ref: In the style of synthesized sirens
sounds.blurb: The joystick’s X throws a Papa Srapa’s pitch across octaves and its Y opens the filter: a hand-played siren, whistle or dive.
sounds.how: A Papa Srapa’s cv moves its pitch an octave a volt, and the joystick’s X out spans ±5 V around its offset: across the stick, ten octaves. Small moves are slides and swoops; big ones are whistles and dives. Y goes to CV L, so pushing up brightens it as it climbs.

steps.title: A square tone
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 6: PITCH 5, HI on, FM on, MOD 1, rate 6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 2, RLS 5, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a trilling, whistling square.

steps.title: X on the pitch
steps.why:
Patch the joystick’s X out to Drone 6’s cv. Stick X at −0.2.
- Listen for: the tone a full octave lower; push the stick for sirens.

steps.title: Y on the filter
steps.why:
Patch the joystick’s Y out to CV L. Both FREQ to 5, MOD L and MOD R 2.
- Listen for: the tone darker below the middle and brighter above.

steps.title: Distance
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 4, Y 5, Z 4, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the siren echoing off buildings.

sounds.name: Opening Bloom
sounds.ref: In the style of ambient swells
sounds.blurb: A drone chord whose own slow envelope, patched to the filter, opens it as the chord fades in: a pad that blooms from dark to bright.
sounds.how: A classic drone’s envelope only shapes its volume, but its env out lets it do more. Patched into CV L, it opens the filter as the voice fades in and closes it as it fades out, so the chord brightens as it swells, as an acoustic sound does.

steps.title: A slow chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: C2, G2, D4, E4, B5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE, ATT 8, RLS 8, VOL 9, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a C major ninth swelling in slowly.

steps.title: Close the filter
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 2.5, RES 3.
- Listen for: the chord muffled.

steps.title: Let it bloom
steps.why:
Patch Drone 1’s env out to CV L. MOD L and MOD R 5.
- Listen for: the chord brightening as it swells and darkening as it fades.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the bloom in a large space.

context.d1.att: In this sound: how slowly the chord swells and opens.

sounds.name: Jet Drone
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s psychedelic jet flanging
sounds.blurb: Two classic drones, one each side, swept by VIBE’s resonance flanger: a roaring, jet-plane whoosh moving through a chord.
sounds.how: A flanger mixes a sound with a copy of itself delayed by a few milliseconds that moves, and with feedback the comb it makes rings. On a thick, steady drone it is a jet passing overhead. VIBE’s third program is the resonant one: X is its feedback, Y its speed and Z its depth.

steps.title: Two drones

sounds.name: Just Intonation
sounds.ref: In the style of La Monte Young — “The Well-Tuned Piano”
sounds.blurb: A classic drone’s five generators tuned to pure, whole-number ratios: a major seventh chord with no beating at all, stiller and brighter than a keyboard can play.

sounds.name: FM Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s FM synth basses
sounds.blurb: VCO A, unheard, frequency-modulates VCO B through the 42N’s normal: a bright, slappy, metallic bass of the kind 80s FM synths made famous.
sounds.how: VCO B’s cv input hears VCO A with nothing patched in, so CV AMT is an FM depth knob. With both on sine at the same pitch, VCO A adds harmonics to VCO B the way an FM synth’s modulator does its carrier: a bright, clean, slightly metallic tone. VCO A’s own channel stays down.

steps.title: A sine bass
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0, VCO B VOL 8. Both on sine. Envelope B: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 3, RELEASE 2.
- Listen for: a pure, round bass.

steps.title: Modulate it
steps.why:
VCO B’s CV AMT 3.
- Listen for: the bass turning bright, twangy and metallic.

steps.title: Open up
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 7.5.
- Listen for: all the new harmonics through.

context.vb.cvamt: In this sound: the FM depth, how bright and metallic the bass is.

tweaks.hear: A harsher, clangier tone.
A different ratio: an inharmonic, bell-like bass.

sounds.name: Industrial Grind
sounds.ref: In the style of late-70s industrial music
sounds.blurb: Both Papa Srapa voices, one chopped into a fast mechanical grind and one a low droning square, driven hard through the distortion: a factory floor.
sounds.how: Early industrial music made its noise from oscillators, tape and distortion with no wish to be pretty. Drone 3 mixes noise with a low tone chopped by AM at a buzzing rate; Drone 6 is a low square under it; both go through a band-pass filter, moved by LFO A, and the distortion at its hardest.

steps.title: The machine
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 3: PITCH 3, NOISE 5, AM on, 1 / 10 on, rate 6. Drone 6: PITCH 2, VOL 5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to both GATEs. ATT 1, RLS 4 on both. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: a buzzing, chopped grind over a low drone.

steps.title: Crush it
steps.why:
Both filters BP, FREQ 5, RES 5. DIST 9, GAIN 9. MASTER VOLUME 5.
- Listen for: a harsh, saturated roar.

steps.title: Move it
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R 3, LFO A speed ×6, rate 4.
- Listen for: the grind lurching up and down like a machine under strain.

context.d3.rate: In this sound: the speed of the grind.

tweaks.hear: A slower, pounding machine.
Still grim, but you can hear the parts.

sounds.ref: In the style of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop
sounds.blurb: A pure sine that glides slowly between wide-apart notes, echoing: the swooping, otherworldly tunes of 1960s BBC science fiction.
sounds.how: The BBC Radiophonic Workshop made its tunes from test-tone oscillators, sliding pitches by hand. A sine with long portamento and leaps of an octave or more gives that swooping, unearthly line, and a TIME echo the space of the studio.

- Listen for: each note sliding slowly to the next, overshooting nothing.

sounds.name: Tomita Whistle
sounds.ref: In the style of Isao Tomita — “Snowflakes Are Dancing”
sounds.blurb: A high, whistling tone with a gentle vibrato and a little glide, phased on one side and shimmering on the other: Tomita’s singing synth voices.
sounds.how: Isao Tomita arranged Debussy for Moog, giving melodies to whistling, singing synth voices with vibrato and phasing. A triangle an octave up with a touch of portamento whistles; LFO B gives the vibrato; VIBE’s phaser on the left and CATHEDRAL on the right put it in a dreamlike space.

steps.title: A whistle
steps.why:

- Listen for: a high, pure whistle gliding a little between notes.

- Listen for: a singing waver.

sounds.name: House Organ Bass
sounds.ref: In the style of early-90s house organ basslines
sounds.blurb: A punchy, bouncing organ bass: square with its sub, a click on top, short and staccato, as on early-90s house records.
sounds.how: The early-90s house organ bass was a preset organ played short and bouncy. A square with its sub-oscillator gives the organ, VCO B’s triangle at the same pitch adds the key-click brightness, and a short envelope keeps it staccato.

sounds.name: Lo-fi Keys
sounds.ref: In the style of lo-fi hip-hop
sounds.blurb: Soft, slightly wobbly keys, warm and a little worn, with a chorus: the dusty electric piano of lo-fi hip-hop.
sounds.how: Lo-fi keys sound like an electric piano sampled off old tape: soft, a little out of tune and wobbling. A soft morph wave with VCO B a few cents flat, LFO A nudging VCO A’s pitch for the tape wow, a dark filter, a touch of distortion for saturation and TIME’s Delay chorus.

- Listen for: a soft, slightly chorused electric piano.

sounds.name: Synth Kick
sounds.ref: In the style of the TR-808 kick
sounds.blurb: A sine whose pitch drops fast as it decays, patched from its own envelope: a punchy electronic kick drum.
sounds.how: An electronic kick is a sine that starts high and drops quickly to a low thump. Envelope A, patched into VCO A’s cv, lifts the pitch at the strike and lets it fall as the envelope decays; the same envelope shapes the volume. The keys set the pitch it falls to.

steps.title: A thump
steps.why:
VCO A on sine. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 5.5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 4.
- Listen for: a soft, low thud.

steps.title: The pitch drop
steps.why:
Patch Envelope A’s env out to VCO A’s cv. CV AMT 6.
- Listen for: each thud starting with a click of pitch and dropping: a kick.

steps.title: Punch
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 6. DIST 2, GAIN 5. MASTER VOLUME 8.
- Listen for: a harder, punchier kick.

sounds.name: Synth Snare
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s electronic snares
sounds.blurb: A short tone and a burst of Papa Srapa noise struck by the same key: a crisp, electronic snare drum.
sounds.how: An analogue snare is two things at once: a short tone for the drum’s body and a burst of noise for its wires. VCO A gives the tone, with a little pitch drop from its own envelope; Drone 3’s noise, opened by the keyboard’s gate with no attack and a quick release, gives the snap.

steps.title: The body
steps.why:
VCO A on triangle. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3. Patch Envelope A’s env out to VCO A’s cv, CV AMT 2.
- Listen for: a short, dropping tok.

steps.title: The wires
steps.why:
Drone 3: NOISE 10, ATT 0, RLS 2.5, VOL 10, PAN 0. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. MASTER VOLUME 9.
- Listen for: a crisp burst of noise with each hit: a snare.

steps.title: Room
steps.why:

- Listen for: a bright snare in a small room.

sounds.name: Cowbell
sounds.ref: In the style of the TR-808 cowbell
sounds.blurb: Two square waves a dissonant interval apart, struck short through a band-pass filter: the clanky electronic cowbell of the 808.
sounds.how: The TR-808’s cowbell is two square-wave oscillators at an odd interval, through a band-pass filter, with a short decay. Both of the 42N’s VCOs on square, VCO B six semitones up, both band-pass filters and two short envelopes make the same thing.

steps.title: Two squares
steps.why:
VCO A and VCO B on square. VCO B VOL 7, TUNE 10 (six semitones up).
- Listen for: a clashing, buzzy interval.

steps.title: Strike
steps.why:
Both envelopes: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3.
- Listen for: short, metallic hits.

steps.title: The bell
steps.why:

- Listen for: a hollow, clanky cowbell.

sounds.name: Bagpipes
sounds.ref: In the style of the Great Highland bagpipe
sounds.blurb: A classic drone as the pipes’ three drones, a bass and two tenors on A, and VCO A’s narrow pulse as the chanter playing a tune with grace notes above them.
sounds.how: A Highland bagpipe is three drones, one bass and two tenors tuned in octaves on A, under a reedy chanter that plays the tune and decorates it with very short grace notes. A classic drone is exactly the drones; VCO A’s narrow pulse, quick envelope and a touch of distortion is the chanter.

steps.why:
Drone 1: generator 1 to A1, 2 to A2, 3 to A3, 4 and 5 muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 2, RLS 3, VOL 6, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a buzzing octave drone on A.

steps.title: The chanter
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 2. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 9, RELEASE 1.
- Listen for: a reedy, nasal tune over the drones, with quick grace notes.

steps.title: Reeds
steps.why:

- Listen for: a raw, reedy blare.

steps.title: Outdoors

sounds.name: Tanpura
sounds.ref: In the style of the tanpura drone in Hindustani classical music
sounds.blurb: A classic drone tuned to a tanpura’s Pa and Sa, buzzing and shimmering, with VCO A sliding between notes above it as a singer or sarangi does.
sounds.how: The tanpura is a four-string drone tuned to Pa and three Sas, its bridge making each string buzz with overtones (jawari). A classic drone takes the tuning: Pa below, then Sa in three octaves. A little distortion and a resonant filter slowly moved by LFO A give the buzz and the shimmer. The 42N cannot pluck its generators one by one, so the strings sustain. VCO A plays the melody with portamento for the slides (meend).

steps.title: Pa and Sa
steps.why:
Drone 1: Pa G2, then Sa on C3, C4 and C5; generator 5 muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 4, RLS 9, VOL 7, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a hollow fourth, Pa under Sa, with Sa doubled in octaves.

steps.title: Jawari
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 6, RES 5. DIST 2, GAIN 5. Patch LFO A out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R 2, LFO A rate 4.
- Listen for: the strings buzzing, their overtones shimmering slowly.

steps.title: The voice
steps.why:
VCO A on the sine-to-triangle morph, PW 4, VOL 5. Envelope A: ATTACK 3, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 5. PORTAMENTO 3.5.
- Listen for: a singing line sliding between the notes over the drone.

steps.title: The hall

CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 6, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: the drone and the voice in a warm room.

sounds.name: Didgeridoo
sounds.ref: In the style of the didgeridoo
sounds.blurb: One low, buzzing generator through a resonant band-pass filter that LFO B swings rhythmically up and down: the throaty, pulsing wow-wow of a didgeridoo.
sounds.how: A didgeridoo is one low, buzzing note whose colour the player changes with mouth and throat, in rhythm. A classic drone with one low generator buzzes; a band-pass filter with plenty of resonance is the mouth; LFO B, at a walking pace, moves the formant up and down for the wow-wow; a little distortion adds the lip buzz.

steps.title: One low note
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: generator 1 to D2, the rest muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 2, RLS 4, VOL 9, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a single low buzz.

steps.title: The mouth
steps.why:
Both filters BP, FREQ 4, RES 7. DIST 3, GAIN 6.
- Listen for: a throaty, vocal drone.

steps.title: Wow-wow
steps.why:
Patch LFO B out to CV L, MOD L and MOD R 3. LFO B rate 3.5, wave 0.
- Listen for: the throat opening and closing about once a second.

sounds.name: Preamp Fuzz
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s fuzz-pedal guitar
sounds.blurb: VCO A heard only through the PREAMP, its gain turned far up: a buzzing, sustaining fuzz lead from a channel meant for a contact microphone.
sounds.how: The PREAMP has up to 40 dB of gain for a contact microphone, and it clips when pushed. Patch VCO A’s dry out into its ext. source, turn VCO A’s own channel down and the PREAMP channel up, and VCO A is heard through the preamp alone: with the gain high, it squares off into a fuzz pedal tone. The fuzz happens before the filter, so the filter can tame it.

steps.title: A lead
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 4.
- Listen for: a plain saw lead.

steps.title: Through the preamp
steps.why:
Patch VCO A’s dry out to the PREAMP’s ext. source. VCO A VOL 0; PREAMP VOL 5, PAN 0; PREAMP gain 8.
- Listen for: the lead turned into a thick, buzzing fuzz.

steps.title: Tame it
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5.5, RES 2. TIME on both sides, program 1. X 3, Y 4, Z 4, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: a warm, singing fuzz with an echo.

sounds.name: Drone Stabs
sounds.ref: In the style of techno chord stabs
sounds.blurb: The sequencer’s gate stabs a drone chord in a syncopated rhythm while its cv shifts the top of the chord: a self-playing chord riff.
sounds.how: The sequencer’s gate out can open a drone as easily as an envelope, and its gate switches make a rhythm by leaving some steps silent. Its cv out, into the drone’s CV with MOD on the upper generators, moves the top of the chord on each step. The pulser runs on its own: this sound plays without a key held.

steps.title: A chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: C2, G2, E♭4, G4, B♭5. ATT 0, RLS 3, VOL 8, PAN 0.
- Listen for: nothing yet: nothing opens the drone.

steps.title: Stab it
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE. Gates 2 and 4 off. Pulser 6.5.
- Listen for: a syncopated, stabbing chord riff.

steps.title: Move the top
steps.why:

- Listen for: the top of the chord lifting on some stabs.

steps.title: Dub space
steps.why:

- Listen for: the stabs echoing into a groove.

sounds.name: Echo Throws
sounds.ref: In the style of dub reggae echo throws
sounds.blurb: Each note pushes TIME’s feedback up for as long as it sounds, so the echoes swell after every note and die away in the gaps: a dub engineer’s echo throws, played from the keys.
sounds.how: Dub engineers “throw” a sound into the delay by pushing its feedback up at the right moment. The effector’s cv x moves X, which on TIME is the feedback. Envelope A, patched there, raises it with each note and lets it fall back, so a note’s echoes bloom and then fade on their own.

steps.title: A short note
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 4. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 4, RELEASE 5.
- Listen for: short, hollow notes.

steps.title: A delay
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 3, Y 4, Z 3, BLEND 5. Both FREQ to 5.5.
- Listen for: a few echoes after each note.

steps.title: Throw it
steps.why:
Patch Envelope A’s env out to the effector’s cv x.
- Listen for: each note’s echoes swelling up and then dying away.

sounds.name: Drone Bell FM
sounds.ref: In the style of 1980s FM bells
sounds.blurb: VCO B’s oscillator flickers a drone’s eye at audio rate, so the drone rings with bell-like FM partials that change with each key.
sounds.how: With some light already on its eye, a classic drone’s CV can be pushed both ways. Patch VCO B’s osc out into it and the light swings hundreds of times a second: frequency modulation of every generator whose MOD is on. VCO B follows the keys, so each key gives the drone a new set of partials, bell-like and clangorous, while the drone’s own chord stays put.

steps.title: A drone chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: C2, G2, E4, G4, C6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 0, RLS 6, VOL 8, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a C major chord struck on each key.

steps.title: Some light
steps.why:
MOD on generators 3, 4 and 5. LIGHT 2, CV 4.
- Listen for: the top three raised a little, with room to swing both ways.

steps.title: Ring it
steps.why:
VCO B on sine, VOL 0. Patch VCO B’s osc out to Drone 4’s CV.
- Listen for: the upper chord ringing with metallic, bell-like partials that change with each key.

steps.title: The tower

sounds.name: Melody From the Eye
sounds.ref: In the style of melody over a drone
sounds.blurb: Four generators of a drone hold a chord while the fifth, the only one with MOD on, is stepped by the sequencer into a little melody above it.
sounds.how: A classic drone’s MOD buttons choose which generators the eye can move. With MOD on only the top one, the sequencer’s cv into the CV jack moves just that generator: the drone plays its own melody over its own chord, each step up to six semitones above where it is tuned. The pulser clocks it; the keys open the voice.

steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 2: C2, G2, E3, G4, and generator 5 on C6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 4, RLS 7, VOL 8, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a C major chord.

sounds.name: Two-Axis Filter
sounds.ref: In the style of ambient filter performance
sounds.blurb: The joystick’s X opens the left filter and its Y the right, one low-pass and one band-pass: one hand sculpts the chord in stereo.
sounds.how: CV L is normalled to CV R, but a cable in CV R breaks the normal, so each side’s cutoff can have its own voltage. The joystick has two: X into CV L and Y into CV R. With the left filter low-pass and the right band-pass, moving the stick shapes each side differently: corners of the stick are four different sounds.

steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 5: D2, A2, F♯3, C♯5, E6. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 4, RLS 7, VOL 8, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a D major ninth.

steps.why:

- Listen for: a dark left and a thin, vocal right.

steps.title: Two axes

- Listen for: the shaped chord in a hall.

sounds.name: Quartal Organ
sounds.ref: In the style of 1960s modal-jazz quartal voicings
sounds.blurb: VCO A and VCO B a fourth apart, each with its sub an octave down, through a fast phaser: every key plays a four-note chord in fourths, like a modal jazz organ.
sounds.how: Modal jazz organists voice chords in fourths. Each 42N VCO has a sub-oscillator an octave down; tune VCO B a fourth below VCO A, switch both subs on, and every key sounds four notes: the note, a fourth down, and both an octave lower. A fast VIBE phaser stands in for the rotating speaker.

- Listen for: a hollow, open interval on each key.

steps.title: Stack it
steps.why:

- Listen for: a four-note quartal chord on every key.

steps.title: The rotor
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 6. VIBE on both sides, program 1. X 6, Y 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: a swirling organ.

sounds.name: Vowel Sweep
sounds.ref: In the style of talking synth filters
sounds.blurb: Two saws, one each side, swept together by one LFO through linked filters, low-pass on the left and band-pass on the right: a slow, two-coloured vowel sweep.
sounds.how: The filters’ LINK button makes the right cutoff follow the left, so one voltage moves both. The modes are still each side’s own: with the left low-pass and the right band-pass, one sweep opens the left into a full, bright pad while the right speaks like a slowly changing vowel.

steps.title: Two saws
steps.why:
Both VCOs on saw. VCO B VOL 7, TUNE 5.1. VCO A PAN −5, VCO B PAN +5. Both envelopes: ATTACK 4, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 9, RELEASE 6.
- Listen for: a wide, buzzing pad.

steps.title: Link two modes
steps.why:
Right filter BP. Press LINK. Left FREQ 4, both RES 6.
- Listen for: a dark left and a nasal right, both cut at the same place.

steps.title: Sweep
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to CV L, MOD L 4. LFO A speed ×6, rate 3.
- Listen for: both sides sweeping together: the left opening, the right saying “ooh-aah”.

steps.title: Space
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 1. Z 6, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: the sweep in a large room.

sounds.name: Bee Swarm
sounds.ref: In the style of tone-cluster drone music
sounds.blurb: Two classic drones with their generators bunched around one note, each a few cents apart, their eyes flickered by fast LFOs: a hive of buzzing bees.
sounds.how: A swarm is many buzzing tones close together, each wavering. Two classic drones put three generators each within a fraction of a semitone of G3, plus an octave above, so they beat against each other constantly; LFO B and LFO A, fast and at different rates, flicker the two eyes so every bee wavers on its own. A band-pass filter and a flanger give the buzz its shape.

steps.title: A cluster
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generators 2, 3 and 4 a few cents around G3 and G4, 1 and 5 muted. Drone 2 the same, a little differently. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to both. ATT 4, RLS 5, VOL 10, PANs −3 and +3. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: a dense, beating buzz around G.

steps.title: Wings
steps.why:
MOD on all of both drones’ generators; CV 0.4 on both. Patch LFO B out to Drone 1’s CV (speed ×6, rate 4) and LFO A out to Drone 2’s CV (speed ×10, rate 4).
- Listen for: every bee wavering, fast and unsteady.

steps.title: The hive
steps.why:
Both filters BP, FREQ 6, RES 4. VIBE on both sides, program 2 (Flanger). X 5, Y 3, Z 3, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: a nasal, swirling hum: the swarm moving around you.

sounds.name: Random Filter Steps
sounds.ref: In the style of Berlin-school random filter patterns
sounds.blurb: A held drone chord whose filter jumps to a new random brightness on every pulser tick: the classic sample-and-hold burble, on a chord.
sounds.how: The sample-and-hold filter is one of the oldest synth tricks: random steps on the cutoff, in time. A Papa Srapa’s S&H takes a new sample on each rising edge at its clock input; the pulser, patched there, sets the tempo. Its output into CV L moves both filters, and resonance makes each step ring.

steps.title: A chord
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 4: A1, E2, C4, E4, B5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 3, RLS 6, VOL 8, PAN 0.
- Listen for: an A minor ninth.

- Listen for: a resonant chord.

steps.title: Random steps

- Listen for: the filter jumping to a new place four times a second, each step ringing.

sounds.name: Pocket Calculator
sounds.ref: In the style of Kraftwerk — “Pocket Calculator”
sounds.blurb: Short, clean square bleeps, dry and exact, with a little slapback: the toy-computer melodies of Kraftwerk’s Computer World.
sounds.how: Kraftwerk built Computer World from the plainest electronic sounds: short square beeps with no vibrato and nothing hidden. VCO A on a narrow square with a quick decay and no sustain gives the bleep; a little resonance makes it chirp, and a short slapback echo puts it in a small, clean studio.

sounds.name: Hazy Nostalgia
sounds.ref: In the style of Boards of Canada
sounds.blurb: Two soft saws a little apart, one of them drifting out of tune as if on a stretched tape, dark and chorused: the faded, wobbling warmth of Boards of Canada.
sounds.how: Boards of Canada’s sound is a memory of 1970s television: warm synths played back off worn tape, never quite in tune. VCO A and VCO B are both saws, B a few cents sharp; LFO A slowly pulls VCO A’s pitch, so the pair drift in and out of tune with each other. A dark filter, a touch of distortion for tape saturation and TIME’s Delay chorus finish the haze.

steps.title: Two soft saws
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. VCO B on saw, VOL 6, TUNE 5.1, a few cents sharp. Both envelopes: ATTACK 4, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 6.
- Listen for: a slow, gently beating pad.

steps.title: Stretched tape
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to VCO A’s cv. CV AMT 0.3, LFO A rate 6.
- Listen for: VCO A sagging and recovering every few seconds, the pair drifting apart and back.

steps.title: Worn
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 4.5, RES 2. DIST 2, GAIN 4.
- Listen for: a warm, dark, slightly saturated tone.

steps.title: Haze

sounds.name: Switched-On Bach
sounds.ref: In the style of Wendy Carlos — “Switched-On Bach”
sounds.blurb: A reedy square bass line on the left plates and a bright saw tune on the right, each with its own envelope: two-part counterpoint, as Wendy Carlos played Bach on a modular.
sounds.how: Wendy Carlos recorded Switched-On Bach one line at a time on a Moog modular, giving each voice of the counterpoint its own timbre. The 42N’s SPLIT mode does it live: the lower plates play VCO A, the upper plates VCO B. A hollow square takes the bass and a bright saw the tune, each with its own crisp envelope, in a small hall.

steps.title: Split the keyboard
steps.why:
The display to SPLIT. The plates left of the middle now play VCO A; those right of it play VCO B.
- Listen for: the bass and the tune coming from different voices.

steps.title: A reedy bass

VCO A on square, PW 5, VOL 7, PAN −2. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 2.

- Listen for: a brassy line above the bass, a little to the right.

sounds.name: Filter House
sounds.ref: In the style of French house
sounds.blurb: A syncopated minor-seventh chord stab from two classic drones, the filter swept open and shut by an LFO and phased: the filtered-disco loop of French house.
sounds.how: French house took a few bars of a disco record and swept a resonant filter across them, over and over. Two classic drones, tuned to an E minor seventh between them and opened by the keys with no attack and a short release, play the stabs. LFO A sweeps both filters, and VIBE’s Phaser adds the swirl.

steps.title: A chord between two drones
steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 1: generator 1 muted, then E2, B3, D5 and G5. Drone 2: generators 1 and 5 muted, then E3, G4 and B4.
- Listen for: nothing yet: both voices are closed.

steps.title: Stab it
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to Drone 1’s GATE and Drone 2’s GATE. ATT 0, RLS 3 on both, VOL 7, PANs −2 and +2. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: short, syncopated chord stabs.

steps.title: The sweep
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to CV L. Both FREQ to 4, RES 5, MOD L and MOD R 3. LFO A speed ×6, rate 3.
- Listen for: the stabs opening up bright and closing to a muffled thud, over and over.

steps.title: Swirl
steps.why:
VIBE on both sides, program 1 (Phaser). X 4, Y 3, BLEND 4.
- Listen for: a slow phasing swirl over the sweep.

sounds.name: Octave Sequence
sounds.ref: In the style of Giorgio Moroder — “I Feel Love”
sounds.blurb: A fast sixteenth-note bass bouncing between the root, the octave and the fifth, driven by the pulser: the hypnotic sequenced bass of Moroder’s disco.
sounds.how: Giorgio Moroder built "I Feel Love" on a Moog sequencer playing a bass that jumps between the root and the octave every sixteenth note. Here the 42N’s own sequencer, four stages long, gives the root, the octave, the fifth and the octave again; the pulser runs it at about eight steps a second, and the keys set the root it transposes from.

steps.title: A plucked saw
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 3.5, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 2.5. Both FREQ to 5, RES 4.
- Listen for: a short, dark pluck on each key.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.why:
Stages 4. Steps 0, 2, 1.17, 2: the root, the octave, the fifth and the octave. Pulser 8.1.
- Listen for: nothing yet: the sequencer is not patched.

steps.title: Run it
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s cv out to VCO A’s 1v/oct and its gate out to Envelope A’s gate.
- Listen for: a driving bass bouncing between octaves, moving with each new key.

steps.title: Space

sounds.name: Ciani Bubbles
sounds.ref: In the style of Suzanne Ciani — “Seven Waves”
sounds.blurb: Round, wet blips at random pitches, bouncing between two different echoes: the liquid, bubbling Buchla sound of Suzanne Ciani.
sounds.how: Suzanne Ciani’s Buchla music is full of liquid blips flung around the stereo field. A triangle with a quick envelope makes each blip, and a resonant filter gives it a wet edge. Drone 3’s sample and hold, clocked by the pulser, picks a new random pitch for each through VCO A’s cv; the pulser also strikes the envelope. A plain delay on the left and a vibrato delay on the right throw the blips in different directions.

steps.title: A blip
steps.why:
VCO A on triangle. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 3, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3.
- Listen for: a short, round blip.

steps.title: Random pitches
steps.why:
Patch the pulser out to Drone 3’s S&H clock and to Envelope A’s gate, and Drone 3’s S&H out to VCO A’s cv. CV AMT 5, pulser 6.5. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: a stream of blips, each at a new random pitch.

steps.title: Liquid
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5, RES 7.
- Listen for: each blip with a wet, ringing, bubbly edge.

steps.title: Thrown about

sounds.name: Fourth World Horn
sounds.ref: In the style of Jon Hassell — “Fourth World”
sounds.blurb: A soft, breathy horn line doubled a fifth below by a pitch-shifting delay, slow and modal: the treated trumpet of Jon Hassell’s Fourth World music.
sounds.how: Jon Hassell played trumpet through a harmoniser that added voices below his own, so one breathy line became a strange, chord-like horn. VCO A on saw, its filter opened by its own envelope, gives a muted, brassy swell; LFO B a slow vibrato; and MAGIC’s Pitch delay adds an echo a fifth below every note.

steps.title: A muted horn
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. Envelope A: ATTACK 4, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 5. Both FREQ to 3.5, RES 2.
- Listen for: a soft, dark tone that swells in.

steps.title: It opens as it plays
steps.why:
Patch Envelope A’s env out to CV L. MOD L and MOD R 2.
- Listen for: each note blooming brighter as it swells, like breath through a horn.

sounds.name: Night Bus
sounds.ref: In the style of Burial — “Untrue”
sounds.blurb: A soft, deep sine bass under a faint minor chord, with a bed of hiss like rain on a window, all in a huge dark reverb: the lonely, late-night London of Burial.
sounds.how: Burial’s records sound like a city at 3 a.m.: deep sub-bass, distant chords, crackle and rain, all drowned in reverb. VCO A, a sine with its sub on, carries the bass. A classic drone, opened slowly by the keys, holds a quiet minor chord far behind it. Drone 6, held on, is pure noise: the rain. CATHEDRAL’s Space reverb puts it all a long way off.

steps.title: Sub
steps.why:
VCO A on sine, −1 SUB on. Envelope A: ATTACK 1, DECAY 7, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 5.
- Listen for: a soft, deep bass more felt than heard.

steps.title: A distant chord
steps.why:
Drone 4: generator 1 muted, then F2, A♭3, C5 and G5. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 6, RLS 8, VOL 4, PAN 0.
- Listen for: a faint F minor chord welling up behind the bass.

steps.title: Rain

- Listen for: a soft hiss, like rain or worn vinyl, that never stops.

steps.title: Far away

sounds.name: On the Run
sounds.ref: In the style of Pink Floyd — “On the Run”
sounds.blurb: A frantic five-note sequence with a hiss of noise on every step, flanged and racing: the paranoid sequencer run of Pink Floyd’s "On the Run".
sounds.how: Pink Floyd built "On the Run" from a fast EMS sequence and a ticking noise, sent through a flanger. The 42N’s sequencer runs five steps (E, G, A, G, D) on VCO A as fast as about eleven a second. Its gate also opens Drone 3, pure noise with a very short release, for a hi-hat tick on every step. VIBE’s Flanger sweeps it all.

steps.title: A racing line
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 3. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 3, SUSTAIN 2, RELEASE 2. Both FREQ to 5.5, RES 5. Steps 0, 0.5, 0.83, 0.5, 1.67. Pulser 8.7.
- Listen for: one short note: nothing drives the sequence yet.

steps.title: Run it
steps.why:
Patch the sequencer’s cv out to VCO A’s 1v/oct and its gate out to Envelope A’s gate.
- Listen for: a frantic five-note figure.

steps.title: The ticking
steps.why:
Drone 3: NOISE 10, ATT 0, RLS 1.5, VOL 4, PAN +2. Patch a second cable from the sequencer’s gate out to Drone 3’s GATE. On the hardware each jack takes one plug, so sending one output to several inputs needs stackable cables or a multiple.
- Listen for: a hiss of noise on every step.

steps.title: Flanged
steps.why:
VIBE on both sides, program 2 (Flanger). X 6, Y 3, Z 3, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: a jet-like sweep over the run.

sounds.name: Braam
sounds.ref: In the style of film-trailer scores
sounds.blurb: An enormous low brass blast: two detuned saws with a sub, a rumbling drone below, the filter blooming open and the distortion growling, in a vast hall: the trailer "braam".
sounds.how: The "braam" is the huge low brass hit of the modern film trailer, a whole low brass section played at full force and pushed through effects. Two detuned saws with VCO A’s sub, opened by Envelope A through the filter, make the blast; a classic drone adds a rumble two octaves down; distortion makes it growl, and a long reverb makes it vast.

steps.title: Low brass
steps.why:
VCO A on saw, −1 SUB on. VCO B on saw, VOL 7, TUNE 4.9. Both envelopes: ATTACK 1, DECAY 8, SUSTAIN 5, RELEASE 7.
- Listen for: a thick, buzzing low note.

steps.title: Bloom
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 3, RES 3. Patch Envelope A’s env out to CV L. MOD L and MOD R 4.
- Listen for: each hit opening with a brassy blare and closing down.

steps.title: Rumble and growl
steps.why:
Drone 1: C1 and C2 only, the rest muted. Patch the keyboard’s gate out to its GATE. ATT 1, RLS 8, VOL 6, PAN 0. DIST 4, GAIN 6, MASTER VOLUME 6.

steps.title: A vast hall

- Listen for: the blast thundering away into a huge space.

sounds.name: Glide Guitar
sounds.ref: In the style of My Bloody Valentine — “Loveless”
sounds.blurb: A fuzzed pair of oscillators slowly bending in and out of tune, washed in a reverse pitch delay: the woozy "glide guitar" wall of shoegaze.
sounds.how: Kevin Shields of My Bloody Valentine held his guitar’s tremolo arm while strumming, so every chord bent in and out of tune, then buried it in fuzz and reverse reverb. Here a saw and a square a little apart are bent slowly by LFO A on VCO A only, so they wobble against each other; the distortion supplies the fuzz, and MAGIC’s Reverse pitch delay the backwards wash.

steps.title: Two voices
steps.why:
VCO A on saw. VCO B on square, VOL 6, TUNE 5.15. Both envelopes: ATTACK 3, DECAY 6, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 6.
- Listen for: a thick, slightly sour tone.

steps.title: The arm
steps.why:
Patch LFO A out to VCO A’s cv. CV AMT 0.3, LFO A speed ×6, rate 2.
- Listen for: the saw sagging and rising against the square, about once every two seconds.

steps.title: Fuzz

Both FREQ to 5. DIST 6, GAIN 6. MASTER VOLUME 6.
- Listen for: a dense, saturated roar.

steps.title: Backwards

MAGIC on both sides, program 2 (Reverse pitch delay). X 5, Y 7, Z 5, BLEND 6.
- Listen for: a swirling wash behind each note, rising and falling in pitch.

sounds.name: Phase Music
sounds.ref: In the style of Steve Reich — “Piano Phase”
sounds.blurb: Two pulsing tones, one on each side, at almost the same speed, slowly sliding out of step and back in: the gradual phasing of Steve Reich.
sounds.how: Steve Reich’s phase pieces play the same pattern on two instruments, one slightly faster, so they drift apart and slowly realign. The 42N’s two Papa Srapa voices do it on their own: each one’s AM chops its tone at its modulator’s rate. Set the two rates a hair apart and the pulses slide out of step, make new rhythms against each other, and come back together about every fifteen seconds.

steps.why:
VCO A VOL 0. Drone 3: HI on, PITCH 5.58, so its tone sits on E5. AM on, rate 7.4. HOLD on, VOL 6, PAN −4.
- Listen for: a steady beeping on the left, about three a second.

steps.title: A pulse on the right
steps.why:
Drone 6: HI on, PITCH 4.62, B4. AM on, rate 7.45. HOLD on, VOL 6, PAN +4.
- Listen for: a second beeping on the right, almost in step with the first and slowly sliding away from it.

steps.title: Soften them
steps.why:
Both FREQ to 5.5, RES 2. CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3. X 1, Y 3, Z 4, BLEND 3.

sounds.name: Curved Air
sounds.ref: In the style of Terry Riley — “A Rainbow in Curved Air”
sounds.blurb: A fast, bright organ arpeggio fed into a long echo that keeps feeding back, so the patterns pile up into a shimmering, ever-changing web: Terry Riley’s time-lag organ.
sounds.how: Terry Riley played fast modal patterns on an electric organ through a "time-lag accumulator": tape delays that kept feeding back, so each pattern layered over the last. VCO A, a square with a sub and an organ envelope, plays the sequencer’s five notes (a minor pentatonic up to the octave) about eight times a second; TIME’s delay, with a long time and high feedback, stacks them up.

steps.title: An organ
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 5, −1 SUB on. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 3, SUSTAIN 6, RELEASE 1. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: a bright, buzzy organ note.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.why:
Steps 0, 0.5, 1.17, 1.67, 2: the root, minor third, fifth, minor seventh and octave. Pulser 8. Patch the sequencer’s cv out to VCO A’s 1v/oct and its gate out to Envelope A’s gate.
- Listen for: a fast rising arpeggio, round and round.

steps.title: The time lag
steps.why:
TIME on both sides, program 1. X 7, Y 6, Z 3, BLEND 5.
- Listen for: the pattern echoing back over itself, the layers building into a shimmering web.

sounds.name: Silver Apples
sounds.ref: In the style of Morton Subotnick — “Silver Apples of the Moon”
sounds.blurb: A bubbling, unpredictable sequence with odd intervals and a lopsided tempo, the filter jumping at random on another clock: the restless electronic chatter of Subotnick’s Buchla.
sounds.how: Morton Subotnick’s Silver Apples of the Moon, written for the Buchla, is a stream of jumpy sequences whose timbres never settle. Drone 3’s modulator clocks the sequencer at a rate unrelated to anything else; its five steps leap by awkward intervals. The pulser clocks Drone 3’s sample and hold on its own rate and throws the filter to a random place, so the pitch and the brightness change out of step with each other.

steps.title: A chirping square
steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 2. Envelope A: ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 3. Both FREQ to 5, RES 7. Steps 0, 1.83, 0.67, 2.5, 1.
- Listen for: one short, resonant chirp.

steps.title: A lopsided clock
steps.why:

sounds.name: Gamelan
sounds.ref: In the style of Balinese gamelan
sounds.blurb: Bright metallic bars, each one a pair beating against each other, over a low, clanging gong: the shimmering, interlocking sound of a Balinese gamelan.
sounds.how: A Balinese gamelan tunes its instruments in pairs, one slightly higher than the other, so every note shimmers (ombak, "waves"). VCO A and VCO B are the pair, B a touch sharp; VCO B, frequency-modulated by VCO A through its normal, adds the metal. A classic drone tuned low with VOLT past halfway, opened by every note and dying slowly, is the gong.

sounds.how: The koto’s silk or nylon strings are plucked with picks on the fingers, giving a bright twang that quickly mellows; players press the strings behind the bridge to bend notes. VCO A on a narrow pulse, through a resonant filter that its own envelope opens for a moment, makes the twang; a little PORTAMENTO gives the bends; the phrase is in the hirajōshi scale.

sounds.name: Sequenced Hi-hat

sounds.blurb: A crisp, ticking sixteenth-note hi-hat from a burst of noise on every sequencer step, with rests you switch in and out on the gate switches.
sounds.how: A hi-hat is a short burst of very high noise. Drone 3, set to pure noise with no attack and a very short release, is opened by each gate from the sequencer, which the pulser runs at about eight steps a second. High band-pass filters keep only the sizzle. The step gate switches make the pattern: switch one off and that step rests.

sounds.how: The electronic drum pads of the 1980s made toms from an oscillator whose pitch swept down sharply on every hit: the famous “pew” fill. VCO A on sine, its pitch thrown up by its own envelope and dropping as the envelope decays, is the tom; the keys set where each one lands, so a falling phrase is a fill. A little noise from Drone 3 adds the stick.

sounds.name: Helicopter
sounds.ref: In the style of synthesized helicopter effects
sounds.blurb: A thudding rotor chopping the air, a turbine whine on one side, the whole thing slowly passing overhead: a helicopter, from a single self-patched noise voice.
sounds.how: A helicopter’s rotor is a burst of air on every blade pass, a few times a second. Drone 3, set to pure noise, has its own modulator patched back to its GATE: the square opens and closes the voice at the modulator’s rate, so it chops itself. A dark, resonant filter makes each chop a thud; Drone 6’s high tone, held on, is the turbine; LFO A slowly opens and closes the filters as it flies over.

sounds.name: Whistling Filter

The keyboard’s v/oct output, patched into CV L with MOD L and MOD R at full, moves both cutoffs one octave per volt, so the filter follows the keys exactly. FREQ sets where middle C sits. Drone 3, pure noise opened by the keys, is the breath.

sounds.name: Stepped Harmony
sounds.ref: In the style of synth-pop harmonies
sounds.blurb: Every note you play comes with a second note above it, and each new key press brings a different interval (a third, a fifth, a fourth, a sixth, an octave): a harmony that keeps changing.
sounds.how: The keyboard’s gate, patched into the sequencer’s clock, steps it once on every key press instead of on the pulser. Its cv, patched into VCO B’s 1v/oct, adds to the keys’ pitch, so VCO B plays the same note moved by the step: steps tuned to intervals make it a harmoniser whose interval changes with every note. VCO A plays the melody as written.

steps.why:
VCO A on square, PW 4. VCO B on saw, VOL 6. Both envelopes: ATTACK 1, DECAY 5, SUSTAIN 7, RELEASE 4. Both FREQ to 6.
- Listen for: both voices in unison on every note.

steps.title: Intervals
steps.why:
Steps 0.67, 1.17, 0.83, 1.5, 2: a major third, a fifth, a fourth, a major sixth and an octave.
- Listen for: nothing new yet: the sequencer is not patched.

steps.title: Step on each key
steps.why:
Patch the keyboard’s gate out to the sequencer’s clock in, and the sequencer’s cv out to VCO B’s 1v/oct.
- Listen for: VCO B above the tune, a different interval on every note.

steps.title: A hall
steps.why:
CATHEDRAL on both sides, program 3. X 2, Y 3, Z 5, BLEND 3.
- Listen for: the shifting harmonies in a room.

context.seq.stages: In this sound: how many intervals the harmony cycles through.

tweaks.hear: Only the third, fifth and fourth: a tighter, more folk-like harmony.
A minor seventh in place of the octave: a bluesy surprise.
